title: What Does Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning Really Improve in LLM Agents?
trick: Cap the turn budget at evaluation and the RL-over-base gain on agent tasks shrinks or reverses; at matched states RL picks the better action less than half the time, except right after an error.
framing_stripped: Called 'what multi-turn RL really improves' with a 'two-dimensional Pass@(K,T) evaluation', 'mechanistic analyses' and 'BudgetMix RL'; it is (a) a sweep of the maximum-turns cap $T$ at fixed 8 samples per task, on four small environments (FrozenLake, DeepCoder-MT, BFCL-v3, InterCode-SQL) plus Terminal-Bench, for Qwen3-4B/8B trained with GRPO, GiGPO and PPO, showing the RL model falls to or below the base model when $T$ is 25% of the training cap (Table 1, Figure 3); (b) a matched-state action-quality comparison with 16 sampled actions per state, scored by an exact $Q^{*}$ (FrozenLake) or unit-test pass rate (DeepCoder-MT), showing RL wins on 42.8-46.8% of ordinary states and 65.7-67.3% of injected-error states (sec. 3.3); (c) a log-likelihood reading that RL actions stay plausible under the base policy while whole RL trajectories do not (sec. 4.1); and (d) the recipe consequence: sample the training budget uniformly from ten fractions of the cap instead of always training at the cap, which closes most of the tight-budget gap (Table 1).
method_equations: Setting (sec. 2.1): at turn $t$ the agent sees history $h_t = (x, o_1, a_1, \ldots, o_{t-1}, a_{t-1}, o_t)$ for task $x$, samples action $a_t \sim \pi(\cdot \mid h_t)$, the environment returns $o_{t+1} \sim P(\cdot \mid h_t, a_t)$; an episode capped at $T$ turns yields $\tau_{\leq T}$ scored by a terminal verifier $R(\tau_{\leq T}) \in \{0, 1\}$. Metric (eq. 1, sec. 2.2, borrowed from Zhai et al. 2604.14877): $$\mathrm{Pass}@(K,T) = \Pr_{\tau^{(1)}, \ldots, \tau^{(K)} \sim \pi(\cdot \mid x)} \bigl[ \exists i \in \{1, \ldots, K\} : R(\tau^{(i)}_{\leq T}) = 1 \bigr],$$ the probability that at least one of $K$ independent trajectories, each cut off after $T$ turns, succeeds; $\mathrm{Pass}@T := \mathrm{Pass}@(K{=}8, T)$ in every budget sweep (sec. 3.2, App. B.3). $\mathrm{Pass}@K$ is estimated without replacement from $n \geq k$ samples per task, $c$ of them successful: $\widehat{\mathrm{Pass}@k} = 1 - \binom{n-c}{k} / \binom{n}{k}$, swept to $k = 128$ (App. B.2; $n$ not stated). Step quality (sec. 3.3, App. B.4): for a matched state $s$ drawn equally from base and RL trajectories, sample $G = 16$ actions $a_i^{\mathrm{Base}} \sim \pi_{\mathrm{Base}}(\cdot \mid s)$, $a_i^{\mathrm{RL}} \sim \pi_{\mathrm{RL}}(\cdot \mid s)$ and compare the mean action value; on FrozenLake the value is the exact $Q^{*}(s, a)$ from finite-horizon dynamic programming with discount $\gamma = 0.95$ under optimal continuation within the remaining budget, on DeepCoder-MT it is the unit-test pass rate of the submitted program. Depth is $d_t = t / T_{\max} \in [0, 1]$. Likelihood (sec. 4.1): with an action a token sequence $a_t = (w_{t,1}, \ldots, w_{t,m_t})$, $\mathrm{ActionNLL}_{\mathrm{B}}(a_t \mid h_t) = -\sum_{j=1}^{m_t} \log p_{\mathrm{B}}(w_{t,j} \mid h_t, w_{t,<j})$ under the base policy $p_{\mathrm{B}}$, and the cumulative log-likelihood ratio $$\mathrm{LLR}_{1:t}(\tau) = \sum_{i=1}^{t} \bigl[ \log \pi_{\mathrm{RL}}(r_i \mid h_i) - \log \pi_{\mathrm{B}}(r_i \mid h_i) \bigr],$$ where $r_i$ is the whole turn-$i$ response including reasoning tokens; observed on Terminal-Bench: mean action NLL 12.20 (RL actions) vs 10.25 (base actions) under the base policy, cumulative LLR about 228 for successful RL trajectories vs 26 for successful base ones; length-matched (within 10% of tokens) differences 185.9 nats on Terminal (193 pairs, 89 tasks) and 805.8 on BFCL (283 pairs, 146 tasks), App. E.2. Training dynamics (sec. 4.2, App. E.3): $R_{\mathrm{multi}}$ is the trajectory reward being optimised, $R_{\mathrm{single}}$ the mean step value over a fixed pool of 512 base-model states on held-out tasks with 8 actions per state per checkpoint; on DeepCoder-MT $R_{\mathrm{multi}}$ rises by 0.331 while $R_{\mathrm{single}}$ falls by 0.097. BudgetMix (eq. 2-3, sec. 5.2, App. A.4): for task $x$ with full cap $T_{\max}(x)$, $$\mathcal{T}(x) = \mathrm{Unique}\Bigl( \bigl\{ \lceil \tfrac{k}{10} T_{\max}(x) \rceil : k = 1, \ldots, 10 \bigr\} \Bigr), \qquad T(x) \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(\mathcal{T}(x)),$$ one budget per GRPO group of $G = 16$ trajectories, written into the prompt as maximum, completed and remaining turns; a trajectory that exhausts its budget scores 0; the advantage is the standard $A_i = (R_i - \mathrm{mean}(R)) / (\mathrm{std}(R) + \epsilon)$; for GiGPO the anchor is $(s_t, B - t)$ (state plus remaining budget); for PPO budget exhaustion gets zero terminal bootstrap. Caps: $T_{\max} = 70$ (FrozenLake), 10 (DeepCoder-MT), 24 (BFCL-v3), 10 (InterCode-SQL), 50 (Terminal-Bench). Observed (Table 1, $\mathrm{Pass}@8$ in %, budget as a fraction of $T_{\max}$): Qwen3-8B at 25%, base vs GRPO-Full: FrozenLake 34.0 vs 31.9, DeepCoder-MT 42.8 vs 31.5, BFCL-v3 4.8 vs 3.8, InterCode-SQL 29.8 vs 27.0; at 100%: 58.5 vs 78.0, 56.8 vs 66.5, 37.8 vs 45.0, 40.8 vs 49.4. BudgetMix over Full-budget RL, averaged over GRPO, GiGPO, PPO and both sizes: +7.5, +5.3, +4.0 points at 25%, 50%, 75% and 'parity' at 100% (per-cell +1.0 to +1.6).
load_bearing_assumption: That a 25%-of-cap evaluation measures the same thing for the base model and for the RL model, so that the shrinking gap is a property of what RL learned. The protocol undercuts this: the prompt announces the cap and the remaining turns at every step ('Budget-aware prompt template used during training and evaluation', Table 2, App. A.3; 'The budget is specified in the system prompt before generation begins', App. B.1), Full-budget RL only ever saw the prompt with $T_{\max}$ in it ('Standard multi-turn agentic RL samples trajectories under a fixed maximum budget $T_{\max}$', sec. 5.2), and the base model saw none of these prompts in training. A tight-budget evaluation is therefore a prompt the RL model has never been trained on and a cap it has never been scored under, at once; the base model is equally unfamiliar with every budget. The paper never runs the separating control (Full-budget RL evaluated at tight $T$ with the prompt still saying $T_{\max}$, or with no budget line; or an RL run trained without the budget line), so 'RL gains depend on sufficient interaction budget' and 'RL is thrown by a budget counter it never saw' are confounded, and BudgetMix, which trains on every counter value, fixes both at once by construction. Second, that the step-quality verdict transfers: 'RL achieves better step-level decision quality on only 46.8% of DeepCoder-MT states and 42.8% of FrozenLake states' is measured on two environments with an oracle, and the paper itself says 'reliable process rewards remain difficult to obtain in agentic settings' (sec. 3.3), so the headline about step quality rests on FrozenLake and a 10-turn code-resubmission task.
weakest_component: The budget sweep is read at one sampling breadth and one metric: 'we fix the sampling breadth at $k=8$ and vary the maximum interaction turns $T$' (sec. 3.2), Table 1 is $\mathrm{Pass}@8$. $\mathrm{Pass}@8$ is a coverage number that rewards spread across the eight samples as much as per-sample success; RL sharpens the policy (the paper's own Figure 7: successful RL trajectories carry LLR about 228 vs 26), so at tight $T$, where every sample is short and the base model's spread across eight tries is worth most, the metric itself moves against RL. $\mathrm{Pass}@(1,T)$ at tight budgets, the deployment quantity the risk section (sec. 3.4) appeals to, is not reported anywhere in the text, and the joint $(K,T)$ surface is shown only as two one-dimensional slices. Next: (1) the budget is counted in turns, not tokens or seconds, and the length control exists only in the likelihood analysis (App. E.2), not in the $\mathrm{Pass}@T$ sweep; (2) error states are 'proxies rather than rigorous definitions of error states' (App. B.5), made by injecting a random action (FrozenLake) or having Qwen3-1.7B damage the code (DeepCoder-MT), and the matched-state pool is drawn from base and RL trajectories 'to mitigate bias' (App. B.4) with no statement of how many states, so 42.8% and 46.8% have no denominator; (3) no confidence intervals or instance counts are stated for Table 1 or Figures 2-3 (only Figure 6 and 23 carry 95% CIs), training steps and GPU cost are not stated; (4) the process-signal result that is supposed to explain the mechanism runs the other way on realistic tasks: on FrozenLake GiGPO and PPO sit above base at 25% (38.4 and 38.5 vs 30.3, Qwen3-4B) while on DeepCoder-MT both sit below base (28.8 and 29.5 vs 34.0), so 'dense signals fix it where an oracle exists' is one environment; (5) BudgetMix's '+7.5' at 25% is averaged over three algorithms and two sizes on four tasks against a baseline that never saw the evaluation prompt (see load_bearing_assumption).
regime: Models: Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B as base (main); InternVL3.5-8B on FrozenLake and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B on DeepCoder-MT (App. C.2, D.2). Algorithms: GRPO (primary), GiGPO ($\omega = 1$, $\gamma = 0.95$), PPO (critic from the same base, GAE); VeRL; lr $1 \times 10^{-6}$, KL coefficient 0.001 (low_var_kl), $G = 16$ trajectories per task, training temperature 1.0 and top-$p$ 1.0; evaluation temperature 0.6, top-$p$ 0.9 (App. A.2, B.1). Tasks and caps: FrozenLake ($T_{\max} = 70$, generated maps, train/test disjoint), DeepCoder-MT ($T_{\max} = 10$; submit a program, read unit-test feedback, resubmit), BFCL-v3 ($T_{\max} = 24$; trained on EnvFactory executable tool environments), InterCode-SQL ($T_{\max} = 10$; Spider-derived), Terminal-Bench ($T_{\max} = 50$; Tmax training tasks) (App. A.1, A.3). Horizon: 10-70 turns; budgets evaluated at 25/50/75/100% of cap. Pass bands (Table 1, $\mathrm{Pass}@8$, %): base at 100% from 26.4 (BFCL, 4B) to 61.6 (FrozenLake, 4B); GRPO-Full at 100% from 30.2 (BFCL, 4B) to 78.0 (FrozenLake, 8B); at 25% every cell is under 48 and BFCL is 2.5-12.2. $\mathrm{Pass}@K$ swept to $k = 128$. Matched-state study: Qwen3-4B GRPO, $G = 16$ actions per state; error-state continuation success 51.3% vs 38.6% (FrozenLake), 38.5% vs 22.9% (DeepCoder-MT); BFCL error-correction 41.4% (RL) vs 27.2% (base) over 191 tool-call-error prefixes (91 from RL, 100 from base rollouts), App. E.4. Likelihood study on Terminal-Bench and BFCL. Process-signal study (sec. 5.1, App. B.6): oracle $Q$ process reward on FrozenLake, GPT-5.6-Sol as an LLM step judge (0-10 scale) on both. Test-instance counts, training steps, GPU hours, dollar cost: unknown (not in text). Date: arXiv 2026-11-04, v1; venue not stated.
information_asymmetry: (1) Training cap vs deployment cap. The one quantity that decides the paper's headline, the turn cap the deployment will impose, exists at evaluation and is fixed at $T_{\max}$ throughout standard training: 'Standard multi-turn agentic RL samples trajectories under a fixed maximum budget $T_{\max}$ and optimizes either outcome or per-step rewards. However, this objective does not explicitly distinguish solutions that require different amounts of interaction, provided they finish within the budget.' (sec. 5.2). The number of turns a trajectory actually used, $T_i$, is in every training rollout and is discarded by the terminal reward $R \in \{0, 1\}$; a 3-turn success and a 9-turn success under a 10-turn cap get the same advantage. BudgetMix re-injects a coarse version of that information by sampling the cap, but the cap is 'one budget per task group' shared by all $G = 16$ trajectories (App. A.4), so the group advantage still never compares the same task under two caps, and the gradient still cannot see $T_i$ directly. The cheaper training-time quantity, $T_i$ itself (a length-aware reward, or a within-group ranking by turns used), is never tried; the comparison that would settle whether BudgetMix works by budget-sampling, by prompt-distribution matching (see load_bearing_assumption) or by turn-penalty is a 2 x 2 at Qwen3-4B scale on the paper's own four tasks. (2) What $\mathrm{Pass}@(K,T)$ measures and what it cannot see. It is the probability that at least one of $K$ independent trajectories, each cut off at $T$ turns, is scored 1 by the terminal verifier (eq. 1). It integrates over per-sample success and spread across samples, over turns used below $T$, and over whether a failure at $T$ is a wrong commit or an unfinished run. Reported only at $K = 8$ (budget axis) or at $T = T_{\max}$ (breadth axis). It therefore does not report $\mathrm{Pass}@(1,T)$, the single-attempt quantity the deployment-risk argument (sec. 3.4, 'tasks involving irreversible actions') needs; it does not separate 'the RL model needs more turns' from 'the RL model is less diverse across 8 tries'; and it treats budget in turns while tokens per turn are matched only in App. E.2. The RL model's turns-to-success distribution, the per-sample success at each $T$, and the token-per-turn length are all in the same rollouts and are not reported. (3) Step oracle at evaluation vs no step signal at training. The exact $Q^{*}(s, a)$ under the remaining budget (FrozenLake) and the per-turn unit-test pass rate (DeepCoder-MT) exist at evaluation and are used as a ruler (sec. 3.3) and once as an oracle process reward (sec. 5.1), while standard training sees only $R_{\mathrm{multi}}$; the paper documents $R_{\mathrm{single}}$ falling by 0.097 while $R_{\mathrm{multi}}$ rises by 0.331 on DeepCoder-MT (sec. 4.2) and states the generalisation gap: 'such precise process supervision is rarely accessible in realistic agent tasks' (sec. 5.1); 'even a strong judge model cannot consistently provide high-quality process supervision across all tasks, particularly in more realistic settings such as BFCL' (App. B.6). The step-quality decline is thus measured where an oracle exists and asserted where it does not. (4) Hindsight-made errors vs natural errors. Recovery is measured on error states built after the fact by injecting a random worse action or an LLM-damaged program ('Both constructions serve as proxies rather than rigorous definitions of error states', App. B.5); the errors the RL policy itself makes and recovers from in deployment, and whether its recovery advantage holds on those, are in the rollouts and not isolated; the matched-state pool mixes base- and RL-visited states to 'mitigate bias' but the state-visitation difference itself (which states RL steers into) is never reported. (5) Per-trajectory vs per-model. Everything in Table 1 is a per-model mean over unstated numbers of instances and 8 samples, without CIs; the single-run spread that CL-W43-14 names is absent here too. For the lane: this is the first paper in hand that reads 'what RL changed' through an evaluation axis (turn cap) rather than a recipe, and it leaves the definitive comparison undone: standard RL vs BudgetMix vs turn-penalised RL vs budget-blind RL, each evaluated at $\mathrm{Pass}@(1,T)$ and $\mathrm{Pass}@(8,T)$ with the budget line held fixed or varied, on the paper's own four environments at 4B.
occupies: Published: the finding that outcome-only multi-turn RL (GRPO, GiGPO, PPO on Qwen3-4B/8B) beats its base model at $\mathrm{Pass}@K$ up to 128 and at $\mathrm{Pass}@8$ with the full turn cap, but falls to or below the base at 25% of the cap on FrozenLake, DeepCoder-MT, BFCL-v3, InterCode-SQL and Terminal-Bench, with structural upper bounds showing headroom remained (App. B.3); that at matched states RL picks the better action on 42.8-46.8% of ordinary states and 65.7-67.3% of injected-error states with higher continuation success from errors; that RL actions are plausible under the base policy while RL trajectories are not (cumulative LLR about 228 vs 26); that $R_{\mathrm{single}}$ declines while $R_{\mathrm{multi}}$ rises during training; that oracle process rewards and GiGPO stabilise budgets on FrozenLake but not on BFCL/DeepCoder-MT; and the BudgetMix recipe (uniform cap from ten fractions, one per group, cap and remaining turns in the prompt) with +7.5/+5.3/+4.0 points at 25/50/75% and parity at 100%. Not claimed and left open: $\mathrm{Pass}@(1,T)$ at any budget; the control separating budget-prompt distribution shift from budget dependence; a turn-penalty or turns-used reward as the alternative to budget sampling; token-matched budgets; confidence intervals or instance counts on the sweep; any model above 8B; natural (non-injected) error recovery.

neighbors.title: Does RL Expand the Capability Boundary of LLM Agents? A PASS@(k,T) Analysis
neighbors.trick: Vary both the number of samples $k$ and the interaction depth $T$ for tool-use agents and show the RL pass curve pulls above the base model's and widens at large $k$ on compositional information-gathering tasks, with SFT on matched data regressing the boundary; this paper takes its metric from there ('prior work introduced Pass@(K,T) to characterize multi-turn capability boundaries', sec. 6.2) and adds the budget-dependence, step-quality and training-dynamics readings.

neighbors.title: Does Reinforcement Learning Really Incentivize Reasoning Capacity in LLMs Beyond the Base Model?
neighbors.trick: Measure pass@k at large $k$ for RLVR models on math, code and visual reasoning and find the base model overtakes at large $k$, so RL reweights what the base could already reach; this paper's Takeaway 3.1 is the multi-turn counter-result ('This contrasts with prior observations in single-turn tasks, where RL does not expand capability boundary beyond the base model', sec. 3.1) and borrows its unbiased pass@k estimator (App. B.2).

neighbors.title: Group-in-Group Policy Optimization for LLM Agent Training
neighbors.trick: Keep GRPO's trajectory-level group advantage and add a step-level advantage by grouping actions taken from repeated environment states across the group's rollouts, giving per-step credit with no critic or extra rollouts; here it is the dense-signal arm that stabilises tight budgets on FrozenLake, where states recur, and not on DeepCoder-MT, where 'recurring matched states are difficult to obtain' (App. E.1), with anchors extended to (state, remaining budget) under BudgetMix (App. A.4).

neighbors.title: Verified Critical Step Optimization for LLM Agents
neighbors.trick: Start from failed trajectories, let a process reward model nominate critical steps, have expert models propose alternatives, keep only those the policy itself can execute to success, and train on them with DPO, supervising 16% of steps; cited here for the premise that 'reliable process rewards remain difficult to obtain in agentic settings' (sec. 3.3), which is why step quality is measured only where an oracle exists.

neighbors.title: Why Multi-Step Tool-Use Reinforcement Learning Collapses and How Supervisory Signals Fix It
neighbors.trick: Trace abrupt collapses in tool-use RL to probability spikes on specific control tokens that break the call format while the underlying ability survives, and show interleaving SFT with RL stabilises training at a cost in out-of-distribution robustness; this paper (same group) cites it among 'mechanistic analyses' of multi-turn agents (sec. 6.2) and positions its own likelihood reading as the step-vs-trajectory shift rather than a format failure.

theme_fit.why: directly asks what changes when agents are trained with RL over long horizons (step quality vs recovery vs trajectory success, read against the turn cap and across training checkpoints) and compares GRPO, GiGPO and PPO on the same tasks; it is a measurement with a small recipe consequence, and the definitive comparison it leaves undone (budget-prompt control, Pass@(1,T), turn-penalty arm) is lane-shaped and under one GPU-week at 4B

supplies an evaluation instrument (Pass@(K,T) with a turn cap) and an effort-sensitivity result: the RL-vs-base ranking flips with the budget, and the metric's coverage-vs-single-attempt reading at K=8 is exactly the lane's 'where the measurement fails' question
turn budgets are counted, never costed; no serving or rollout-system content

limitations_as_complaints: My tight-budget evaluation hands the RL model a prompt it never trained on and a cap it was never scored under, both at once, while my base model is equally unfamiliar with every budget, so I cannot say how much of the collapse is budget dependence and how much is a counter the model never saw: 'Budget-aware prompt template used during training and evaluation' (Table 2); 'Standard multi-turn agentic RL samples trajectories under a fixed maximum budget $T_{\max}$' (sec. 5.2); 'Full-Budget and BudgetMix RL use identical training settings; their only difference is the distribution of budgets' (App. A.2) [paraphrase: no run trains without the budget line or evaluates with the line held at $T_{\max}$].

I measure step quality only where an oracle exists and then assert the decline everywhere: 'Strictly evaluating one-step quality is challenging because reliable process rewards remain difficult to obtain in agentic settings' (sec. 3.3); 'even a strong judge model cannot consistently provide high-quality process supervision across all tasks, particularly in more realistic settings such as BFCL' (App. B.6); and my error states are 'proxies rather than rigorous definitions of error states' (App. B.5) made by injecting a random action or an LLM-damaged program, not the errors the policy makes itself.

My whole budget story is read at eight samples per task and never at one: 'we fix the sampling breadth at $k=8$ and vary the maximum interaction turns $T$' (sec. 3.2); Table 1 reports '$\mathrm{Pass}@T$ evaluation results ($\mathrm{Pass}@8$, %)', while the risk I warn about is single-attempt deployment with 'irreversible actions' (sec. 3.4) [paraphrase: $\mathrm{Pass}@(1,T)$, confidence intervals and instance counts for the sweep are not in the text].
